speaker: robinnorris
text: Thank you very much, Chief Justice Rodriguez. And may it please the court, my name is Robin Norris. I represent Moses Jack Popp, who was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because he was under the age of 18 at the time of the commission for which he was convicted. I have brought to the court seven points of error because of time constraints. I'm going to emphasize some more than others, but I'm pleased to engage with the court on any which are of particular interest to you. And I urge you, I know you will, to interrupt me at any point with questions about any one of the points of error, no matter which order they occur in. Let me begin with the first two issues, which of course are the most controversial, and I really have elected not to spend too much time on them unless there are certain questions of interest to the court. This involves a pretrial motion to quash the indictment based upon failure to allege certain critical theories of culpability upon which we suspected the state would rely. This issue is an old issue, and I tried in my brief as succinctly as I could to develop a history based upon the Penal Code of 1974, which created what people call the party's theory of culpability, actually a theory of vicarious culpability in which a person can be convicted of an offense that he did not commit by his own conduct, but where he was responsible for the conduct of another. That section of the Penal Code contains particular conduct elements which are never alleged or at least have been very uncommonly alleged since 1974 in indictments. I have a complaint that they did not provide adequate notice for that reason. The case was initially controlled, I think, as early as 1975 by Pitts v. State, and I have tried to illustrate in my brief how contemporaneous issues involving similar questions of law were resolved differently. I've tried to frame for the court the issue that Pitts is contrary to the normal way in which such issues, excuse me, are resolved, and I just want to emphasize the importance of having the court specifically address the argument I make, which I do not believe has been addressed before by the Courts of Appeals, certainly not by the Court of Criminal Appeals, and that is that Pitts is contrary to other cases. The example I give and rely upon most as an analog is Jeter, which has to do with the allegations of elements in theft cases where lack of consent is based upon deception, but there are multiple other examples. I just want to insist and hope that the court will confront directly my argument that Pitts is in conflict with these other cases and that it should be resolved in my favor, but if it isn't, to have an explanation from the court why it isn't. Let me move on then to issues number four and five. These have to do with a complaint, first about the admissibility of, but particularly with the failure of the court to provide a limiting instruction at the time evidence of an extraneous offense was admitted into evidence over into evidence over objection. This, again, is something that is almost a no-brainer to me. The law has been pretty clear almost time out of mind, certainly for decades now, that when, particularly, a defense attorney has an objection to the admissibility of an extraneous offense and that evidence is admitted over objection, that it must be received for a purpose, of course, other than character conformity, which means that it must be limited in the jury's consideration, and it should be limited not only to exclude consideration for character conformity, but also to identify the particular purpose for which it's being received. I made a request for that. In this case, it was denied, and so that was an error, and it would be an error, but for one single exception, and that is for what's called same-transaction contextual evidence. I actually have a problem with the law that allows admission without limitation for that kind of evidence because the rules of evidence, excuse me, never allow consideration of extraneous matters for character conformity, even when they're same-transaction contextual evidence, so some limiting instruction, in my view, ought to be required even when to exclude consideration for character conformity, even under those circumstances, but here, it seems fairly clear to me that this doesn't qualify as same-transaction contextual evidence, excuse me, anyway, because it was not so connected the offense being prosecuted that the jury would not, excuse me, be able to understand it without proof of the extraneous offense as well. The state has argued that it is same-transaction contextual evidence. We disagree, and I think the disagreement is based upon real clarity in the record that it was not connected. Certainly, the state would have prosecuted Mr. Popp even without the extraneous offense. They would have sought a conviction and would have believed they were entitled to it, and they most likely would have obtained it,

But, I mean, your starting point is the code and the penal code, section 701 C, states that the state is not required to allege the law of parties in the indictment. And, you know, subsequently to that Pitts, the court of appeals in Pitts stated that, you know, when you have an offense where you're charging someone as a principal or a party, they may be charged as a party without alleging the facts which make the defendant a party to the offense. Now, you know, court subsequent to that, including the court of criminal appeals has affirmed that holding. And I know that the appellant has argued that that's somehow inconsistent with the line of cases talking about constitutional statutory requirements for pretrial notice. But, and I think in the reply brief said that we did not actually address that argument. But the argument is there is no inconsistency because the law is pretty clear. Because the law is clear, the cases that he has cited regarding the pretrial notice are just simply not applicable. And that would be the response to that argument. And since the state wasn't required to plead the law parties in the indictment, the trial court didn't err in denying the motion to dismiss the indictment on that basis. Now, we go ahead and also discuss that, you know, even if for some reason we were required to plead the law parties, you know, the appellant, none of his substantial rights were prejudiced because he received adequate notice of what the theories of parties liability would be at the hearing on the pretrial motion to dismiss the indictment. We specifically, when telling the judge, you would just, the court, that they would just need to charge the jury on two of the parties theories, we identified the aiding theory and the conspiracy theory. You know, we also said that this was a common scheme that the, that the two defendants were out there robbing people that night that should have also put them on notice of the two theories that we would be relying on if it was raised by the evidence. I think if you look at the record as a whole, it's apparent that defense counsel was more than prepared. They even during the plea discussions right before, I think jury selection discussed the law parties with the appellant and defense counsel will say that they had already discussed the law parties with the appellant and the appellant acknowledged that that had actually happened. So I just don't think that the record as a whole shows any harm or lack of notice because, you know, we didn't plead the law parties in the indictment. And, you know, I don't think that, that we should hold that or that we should say that the trial court erred basically in following the law. Like I said, the law is very clear. The trial court followed the law. The state followed the law real quickly. Issue two is just sort of based on that same premise, which is, you know, courts of this state, the law is pretty clear that that the court can go ahead and charge the jury on parties liability, even if, you know, none of that was pled in the indictment. So that would not have the, that would not have made the jury charge erroneous to go ahead and include parties instructions in the charge. Now, with respect to the complaints about the extraneous offense limiting instructions in the complaint in issue four, the appellant complains about not getting the contemporaneous extraneous offense limiting instruction. We of course, you know, made the argument that no instruction, and this applies to issue four and five, no limiting instruction was required because the extraneous offense was same transaction contextual evidence. And the reason for that is when you look at, when you look at the timeline for the two offenses, the robbery of the victim in the extraneous offense, which was Desiree Guerrero, that occurred at approximately 1246 AM, approximately. Then according to the text messages, the defendant started texting the victim in this case at about 147 AM. So you're looking at about an hour's difference in time. They occurred consecutively. They're similar in their manner of execution, right down to how they set up the drug deal and the language that they used. And so the cases that we cited in the brief have to do with the same transaction contextual evidence in crime spree cases. And the premise there is that, you know, offenses that occur so close in time during a crime spree is usually part of the story. So the story here for the state is that on that night, the defendant, these two defendants were going around setting up drug deals and robbing drug dealers. That was the scheme. It just so happens that the second victim was murdered. So we would argue based on the cases that we cited, this is same transaction contextual evidence in which case the trial court was not required to give a limiting instruction either contemporaneously or in the jury charge. Now we went ahead and argued also that with respect to the request for contemporaneous limiting instruction, that it was not clear from the record whether or not the trial court ever made a blanket refusal to give a contemporaneous limiting instruction. So I'm just not sure that the record is clear that there was an adverse ruling in the sense that the trial court decided that it was just not going to give any kind of instruction at all under these circumstances. But we also argue that, you know, even if there was some error in that regard and it was preserved, that the record doesn't support a finding of harm because the jurors were expressly informed prior to deliberations that they were not to form an opinion about the case before they had heard everything. I think if you look at, if you look at the closing arguments especially, you know, Appellant's closing argument, the defense counsel actually told the jury, look, he's, the defendant is entitled to be tried for this offense only and that, and they said that we put on the extraneous offense just to make him look bad, but that the only offense that he was being charged with was the murder in this case. Additionally, we mentioned the extraneous offense, but we made it clear, and I disagree with the appellate counsel, that the state never identified the purposes for which we were relying on that evidence. We specifically said at various points in time that we were relying on that evidence for purposes of identity, intent, motive, opportunity, knowledge, and rebuttal of a defensive theory, and that's basically what we argued during the closing arguments, and also, you know, those are permissible purposes under Rule 404b. There's no evidence at all that the jury formed an opinion about any of this before deliberating, and so for those reasons, we would argue that any decision not to give the contemporaneous limiting instruction was harmless. Now, with respect to the instruction in the charge and the complaint that it wasn't the limiting instruction in charge and that it was not sufficiently limited to the 404b purposes for which the evidence was offered, I cited a handful of cases in the brief that hold that it is not error to include potentially non-applicable 404b purposes so long as the ones that were actually included in the charge are supported by the evidence, and there are a number of these that are, in fact, supported by the evidence, and those cases hold that anything that doesn't really apply can be disregarded as surplusage and just disregarded by the jury as not being applicable.
